title: Lesson 5: Close Read-aloud, Session 4: What Makes Day and Night
objective: Students will learn to distinguish information from illustrations and text about the pattern of light and dark on earth, describe the location of the sun, moon, and stars using prepositions, and record observations in writing using descriptive language.

what_is_taught.skill: distinguish information learned from illustrations versus text
describe the pattern of light and dark on earth
identify and define nouns, verbs, adjectives, and prepositions in a poem
use gestures and hand motions to represent meaning of poem verses
repeat poem verses with expression and varied voices
take notes using pictures and words to record key ideas about day and night
use sentence frames to support writing about day and night
participate in shared writing to reflect on guiding questions and patterns in the sky
use descriptive adjectives to write about the sun in a notebook
describe the location of the sun using prepositions in shared writing

what_is_NOT_taught: Advanced grammar beyond nouns, verbs, adjectives, and prepositions

student_actions.recognition_identification: identify nouns, verbs, adjectives, and prepositions in a poem and text
student_actions.oral_production: answer questions about the poem and text, participate in partner talk, repeat poem verses with expression, share ideas during group discussions
student_actions.written_production: write notes using pictures and words about day and night, write sentences describing the sun in a notebook, contribute to shared writing about the sun's location
student_actions.procedural_application: use sentence frames to complete writing tasks
student_actions.representation_modeling: use gestures and hand motions to represent poem verses
student_actions.reasoning_explanation: explain meanings of text chunks and patterns in the sky, discuss how illustrations and text provide information
student_actions.comprehension_response: answer questions about the poem's meaning and the pattern of light and dark on earth, respond to prompts about observations in the sky and the sun's location in pictures, reflect on guiding questions orally and in writing, distinguish information from illustrations and text in a book

evidence.quote: Tell students that you will recite the poem first on your own as they listen. Say: 'As I read the poem, I want you to think about what the poem is about.'
Read aloud the entire poem, slowly, fluently, with expression, and without interruption.
'What is the poem about?' (where the sun, moon, and stars are in location to other things like buildings, ground, trees)
Invite students to whisper a noun from the poem, 'Where Are They: The Sun, Moon, and Stars', into their hands. Then invite them to whisper a verb from the poem into their hands.

Affirm that this poem describes where sun, moon, and stars are in location to other things. Tell students that words that describe where things are located in relation to other things have a special name, prepositions. Define preposition (a word that describes the location of one thing in relation to another thing).

'What are some hand gestures, motions, or actions that go along with each verse of the poem?' (Answers will vary, but might include: lifting their arms slowly to show the sun rising up over the horizon, sun high in the sky, full moon coming up over buildings.)

Reread the poem aloud a second time and invite students to repeat each verse after it is read, using their own chosen gestures and hand motions. Tell students that they will continue to work with this poem over the next several lessons to describe where the sun, moon, and stars are located.

As students practice the poem with gestures, provide options for expression by echoing several times in different voices. (Example: Invite students to try repeating each verse in a whisper voice, in a giant voice, and/or in an opera voice.) (MMAE)
I can distinguish what I learn from the illustrations and what I learn from the text in the book What Makes Day and Night to describe the pattern of light and dark on earth.

Reduce barriers to comprehension by activating relevant prior knowledge of the learning target. Invite students to recall previous close read-aloud sessions in which they identified learning from the illustrations and from the text to describe light and dark on earth. (MMR)
'What does this sentence mean?' Responses will vary.)
'What, in the illustrations, help you understand that information? What, in the text, helps you understand that information?' (Responses will vary.)
'Can you use a direction word to complete the sentence frame: The earth is moving you ______?' (around in space; away from the sun; toward the light)
'I can distinguish what I learn from the illustrations and what I learn from the text in the book What Makes Day and Night to take notes on the pattern of light and dark on earth.'
'What does it mean to take notes?' (short, written-down words to help us remember something)

Tell students they will use their own notes sheet to capture quick notes about the pattern of light and dark that we call day and night. Tell students that they will use these notes in the next lesson during the Science Talk protocol. Students can use pictures and words to record their notes.
Invite students to begin working.
Provide sentence frames as needed:
Refocus students whole group and invite a few students to share out their notes.
Invite students to stretch their hands up to the sky as if they are touching the sun as they transition.
'What is the pattern?' (light and dark on earth, which we call day and night)

'How does our discussion add to your understanding of how to answer the guiding question: What patterns can we observe in the sky? I'll give you time to think and discuss with a partner.' (Responses will vary.)
I can record my observations from images/videos of the sky in my Sky Notebook.
'What does the sun look like?'

Students should answer the question using pictures and words to show their thinking. Remind students to use the Adjectives anchor chart to describe what the sun looks like. Remind students to use a complete sentence when answering the question.
Transition students to their workspaces and invite students to begin working on page 3.
Refocus students whole group.
-Point to the prompt at the top and read aloud: 'Where do we see the sun?'
-Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group.

-As students share responses, use their ideas to answer the prompt. Begin by circling one of the pictures that most closely resembles the location of the sun in the photograph and then model writing a complete sentence to describe the location of the sun. (Example: 'The sun is over the building.')
Give students specific, positive feedback for their work helping to describe the position of the sun and tell them that they will write about the position of the moon during the next lesson.

teacher_actions.direct_instruction: Teacher models fluent, expressive reading of the poem and models writing a complete sentence describing the sun's location. Teacher defines nouns, verbs, adjectives, and prepositions. Teacher guides close read-aloud and note-taking procedures. Teacher facilitates shared writing and provides sentence frames.
prompts_that_cue_student_response: What are some hand gestures, motions, or actions that go along with each verse of the poem?
What, in the illustrations, help you understand that information? What, in the text, helps you understand that information?
Can you use a direction word to complete the sentence frame: The earth is moving you ______?
What does it mean to take notes?
How does our discussion add to your understanding of how to answer the guiding question: What patterns can we observe in the sky?
What does the sun look like?
Where do we see the sun?

scope.breadth: Focus on understanding the pattern of light and dark on earth and describing the location of sun, moon, and stars using prepositions; includes reading, discussion, note-taking, and writing.
scope.depth: Students engage in close reading, oral discussion, note-taking with pictures and words, and shared writing to deepen understanding of informational text and descriptive language.

context.stimulus_provided: text, images, anchor charts, poem, photographs
